You use idiomatic pronominal verbs: farcela (to manage), andarsene (to leave), cavarsela (to get by), prendersela (to take offence), metterci and volerci (to take time, to be needed), smetterla (to stop).
to get upset, to take offence
I can't manage on my own.
How long does it take? It takes three weeks.
It took me two hours to get here.
Don't get upset, it's not your fault.
To use farcela in all tenses: ce la faccio, ce l'ho fatta, ce la farò.
To use andarsene and its imperative: me ne vado, vattene!, se n'è andato.
To use cavarsela and prendersela: me la cavo, se l'è presa.
To distinguish metterci (who takes the time) from volerci (how much is needed, in general).
To know where the pronouns go: before the conjugated verb, after the infinitive and the imperative.

Florence, September. Bellini has been rushed to hospital. Chiara has to finish on her own the restoration of a processional banner that must be delivered in ten days. It's eleven at night, and only she, Giulia and Matei are left in the workshop.
I can't do it. It's impossible. It takes at least three weeks, and we've got ten days.
Chiara, stop saying "impossible". You managed with the Prato angel, with a fever. You'll manage now too.
With the angel the professor was there. He told me what to do. Now…
Now the professor is in hospital, and if we tell him you got upset, he'll get upset. And a heart patient mustn't get upset.
I'm not upset. I'm scared. It's different.
I know. So let's do this: how long does it take you to clean a square metre of silk?
On my own it takes me two days. With help, maybe one.
Then you're not on your own. Giulia and I are here. And on Saturday Davide's coming too.
Davide is thirteen! Do you feel up to putting an eighteenth-century silk in the hands of a kid?
To hold the lamp, yes. We'll manage, Chiara. We always manage.
All right. But now go to bed, both of you. I'll stay another hour.
One hour. No more. Otherwise tomorrow we'll go to the hospital, to Bellini, and tell him everything.
"non ce la faccio" = I can't manage
"te la sei presa" = you got upset
"quanto ci metti" = how long does it take you
"te la senti" = do you feel up to it
Three words joined into one: che-la-FAT-cho.
Stress on the first syllable, double TT: VAT-te-ne.
"Farcela" = fare + ci + la. It means "to manage, to make it". The particles stay, the verb is conjugated:
Can you manage on your own?
In the passato prossimo the participle agrees with "la": ce l'ho fattA (not "fatto").
Me ne vado. Te ne vai?
Go away! Go away (all of you)!
"Andarsene" stresses that you leave A PLACE (from here). "Vattene!" can be rude; "Me ne vado" is neutral.
The formula is the same: reflexive pronoun (mi→me, ti→te, si→se) + la + verb. Me la cavo, te la cavi, se la cava…
Ci metto due giorni. (It takes me two days.)
Ci vogliono tre settimane. (It takes three weeks.)
Volerci agrees with the thing needed: ci vuole un'ora (singular), ci vogliono due ore (plural). In the passato prossimo: ci è voluta un'ora, ci sono volute due ore.
NOT: "Io ci voglio due ore". When it's about you, use metterci: "Io ci metto due ore."
5. Other useful verbs and the position of pronouns
Non me la sento di guidare.
Pronouns go BEFORE the conjugated verb (ce la faccio), but attach AFTER the infinitive and the imperative (devo farcela, smettila, vattene).
The professor left without saying goodbye.
I get by quite well in Italian.
I don't feel up to driving.
Quanto tempo ci vorrebbe per finire il lavoro?
Con che cosa ce l’ha fatta Chiara in passato?
Quanto ci mette Chiara a pulire un metro quadrato da sola?

It happened on a Saturday morning in mid-September, during the open workshop. Bellini was explaining to a group of German tourists the difference between repainting and retouching, hands behind his back as always, when he suddenly stopped mid-sentence. He leaned on the table. He turned as white as the gesso he used for grounds. Pietro, who was guiding next to him, was the first to notice. "Professor?" he said. Bellini tried to smile. "Nothing, my boy. A little dizzy spell. I can manage." Then he sat down on the floor, slowly, like someone who can't manage any more.

It was Davide who called the ambulance, with a calm nobody expected from a thirteen-year-old. He had learned from his mother: give the address, give the age, give the symptoms, don't hang up. The ambulance arrived in seven minutes. One of the German tourists, who luckily was a doctor, had already knelt beside Bellini and was holding his pulse. "Heart attack," he said in uncertain Italian. "Small, I think. But we must go at once." As the stretcher-bearers carried him away, Bellini managed to say just one thing to Matei: "The banner. The 30th. Don't forget it."

The banner was the most important job of the autumn. It was the silk standard of the San Frediano confraternity, painted and embroidered in the eighteenth century, which every year, on the last Sunday of September, was carried in procession through the streets of the neighbourhood. That year the silk had torn in three places and the colours were flaking. The confraternity had entrusted it to the workshop in June, but between the plaque, the holidays and Aldo's letters, the work had gone more slowly than planned. There were ten days left until the procession. It would have taken at least twenty.

They all spent the afternoon in A&E at Santa Maria Nuova, sitting on plastic chairs, staring at a door that never opened. Rita, Davide's mother, who was on day shifts that week, came out every half hour with news: "They've taken him to the cath lab. They're putting in a stent. The cardiologist is good, the best." Around seven she came out smiling. "He's pulled through," she said. "It went well. He's sleeping now. He'll need a couple of weeks in hospital, and then two months of convalescence. But he'll make it."

Graziella, who until then had sat in silence with her hands clasped in her lap, burst into tears. Then she dried her eyes, stood up and said: "Right. Then tomorrow I'll take him broth. Real broth, not hospital broth." Rita tried to explain that you couldn't bring any food into intensive care. Graziella looked at her the way you look at someone who hasn't understood the situation. "My dear," she said, "I've been taking that man broth for thirty years. I'll manage."

That evening, at the workshop, the race against time began. The banner was spread out on the big table under the lamps, like a patient in an operating theatre. Chiara looked at it with her hands on her hips and an expression Giulia had never seen on her, not even during the fever of the Prato angel. "We can't do it," she said. "It takes three weeks. It took me ten days just to consolidate the first tear. And without the professor…" She didn't finish the sentence. There was no need.

Giulia and Matei looked at each other. They were tired too, and frightened, and their minds were still in the A&E waiting room. But Giulia remembered something Bellini had told her years before, on the first day she walked into that workshop: "Restoration isn't work for heroes. It's work for ants. One millimetre at a time, all together." She said it out loud. Chiara looked at her, then at Matei, then at the banner. "For ants," she repeated. "All right. But then we need more ants."

The ants arrived the next day, one after another, without anyone calling them. Davide turned up at eight with a flask of coffee his mother had made and asked if he could hold the lamps. Valeria Conti, who knew nothing about restoration, offered to answer the phone and deal with the confraternity, "because I can handle people in a hurry". Signor Franco brought an old fan to dry the glue faster. And Pietro organised shifts on a big board hung on the door, with names, times and a rule written in red: "Whoever gets tired goes to bed. Without getting upset."

On the second day the confraternity sent its prior to the workshop, an elderly gentleman with his hat in his hand and a tenor's voice, to find out whether the banner would be ready. Valeria met him at the door with her best smile. "We'll make it," she told him. "But if you come in and start asking questions, it'll take us twice as long." The prior left without coming in, a little offended. He came back the next day with a tray of cantucci made by his wife. Valeria let him in for five minutes. From then on he came every day, with something to eat, and always stayed exactly five minutes.

Meanwhile, in hospital, Bellini was recovering. On the third day they moved him from intensive care to an ordinary ward, and Graziella, who had found a way to smuggle in the broth in a flask labelled "herbal tea", was at last able to sit beside his bed. Bellini was pale, had a thin tube in his nose and looked smaller, as if someone had ironed him. But the first thing he asked was: "The banner?" Graziella had received precise orders from Giulia. "It's going very well," she lied. "They're ahead with the work. You think about getting better, and stop worrying."

Bellini looked at her for a long time. He had known Graziella for thirty years. "You're lying," he said. "I can tell from the way you're holding your bag." Graziella sighed. "All right. They're working day and night. Chiara isn't sleeping. But they're managing, professor. Really." Bellini smiled for the first time since he'd come into hospital. "Then," he said softly, "if they can manage without me, it means I've done my job well. That's what I wanted. I didn't expect it so soon, though."

On the fifth day there was a crisis. Chiara, who was sleeping three hours a night, got the dilution of a consolidant wrong and a small patch of colour, the size of a fingernail, was stained. It wasn't serious, it could be fixed, but Chiara sat in a corner with her head in her hands and said she was leaving, that she wasn't capable, that the professor had been wrong to trust her. Matei tried to talk to her. Giulia tried to talk to her. In the end it was Davide who found the right words, with the simplicity of his thirteen years.

"Chiara," he said, sitting down on the floor beside her, "when I started coming here, I ruined three drawings in one day. The professor didn't get upset. He said: 'Well done. Now you know three ways not to do it.' Now you know one way not to dilute the consolidant. So you're better than yesterday." Chiara looked up at him. Then she burst out laughing, her eyes still wet. "Who taught you to talk like that?" "He did," said Davide. "He says it to everyone. Even to Lupino, when he breaks something."

Chiara went back to work that very evening. She fixed the stain in two hours, with the patience of a watchmaker, and then, instead of going to bed, she stood looking at the banner for a long time. In the middle of the silk was San Frediano holding back the flooding waters of the Arno with a rake, according to the legend. "Think about it," she said to Matei, who was switching off the lamps. "This saint stops the river with a rake. And we complain because we have to stop time with a little brush."

On 29 September, at four in the morning, Chiara made the last retouch. The banner was ready. Not perfect, the professor would have said, but ready, sound, beautiful. Chiara looked at it, then at Pietro's shift board, covered in names, coffee and cantucci. She took the red marker and wrote at the bottom, in big letters: "We made it." Then she lay down on the workshop's little sofa and slept for eleven hours straight, with Lupino at her feet, since nobody had had the heart to send him home.

On Sunday the 30th the procession passed along Via Maggio at eleven. The banner, carried by four men of the confraternity, shone in the sun as if it had been painted the day before. The prior sang in his tenor voice. In front of the trattoria the procession slowed down, and the prior did something that wasn't on the programme: he stopped, turned towards the first-floor window where Chiara, Giulia, Matei and Viola were standing, and made a little bow. The people in the street applauded. Chiara hid behind the curtain, as red as the saint's silk.

That afternoon they all went to the hospital, with photos of the procession on Matei's phone. Bellini looked at them one by one, in silence, his glasses on the tip of his nose. He zoomed in on the photo of the banner, then on the one of Chiara behind the curtain. Finally he put the phone down on the sheets and looked at Chiara. "Signorina Benedetti," he said in his most formal voice, "tomorrow they're discharging me. But it will be two months before I can come back to the workshop. Do you feel up to carrying on like this, without me, until Christmas?"

Chiara looked at Giulia and Matei, who nodded. Then she looked at Davide, who winked at her, and at Pietro, who already had a new shift board in his hand. She took a deep breath. "Yes, professor," she said. "I feel up to it. But on one condition: that you stop working in secret from your bed." Bellini put on the most innocent face in the world. Graziella, without a word, lifted the pillow and pulled out a black notebook full of notes on the banner, written with a trembling hand. "There," she said. "I knew it. I'm taking this away."

Bellini protested, but without conviction. Then, when the others had gone, he asked Graziella to stay a moment longer. He took her hand. "Graziella," he said, "that day in the workshop, when I sat down on the floor, I thought: this time I won't make it. And do you know what I thought about? Broth. Your broth. I thought that if I went, I'd never eat it again." Graziella squeezed his hand. "Then don't go," she replied. "Because I've still got plenty of broth. And it'll take at least another twenty years to finish it." Bellini laughed softly, and the cardiologist, who was passing in the corridor at that moment, heard him ask whether by any chance the broth in the herbal-tea flask was still warm.

Regole del laboratorio (finché il professore non torna)
One: whoever gets tired goes to bed. Without getting upset and without feeling guilty.
Two: if someone can't manage alone, they ask for help. Nobody's a hero. We're ants.
Three: the prior can come in, but only for five minutes and only if he brings cantucci.
Four: anyone who phones the professor to ask for advice will have Grandma Graziella to deal with.
